newsitem.title: UK: Strong pound undermines UK exports, survey shows.
newsitem.headline: Strong pound undermines UK exports, survey shows.

text.p: The strength of the pound, which has risen in value by nearly a fifth against the deutschemark since last summer, has started to undermine British exports, according to a leading business survey published on Tuesday.

Separate figures from the Bank of England showed broad money supply growth slowed unexpectedly in December but economists said this would not prevent the central bank from pressing for higher interest rates to prevent a resurgence in inflation.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said demand for British manufactured exports had levelled off in the last four months for the first time since October 1993.
Its quarterly industrial trends survey showed manufacturing output grew steadily, but more slowly than expected, in the period.
"The impact of sterling's strength is beginning to feed through to manufacturers' export orders," said Ross Buckland, a member of the CBI's economic affairs committee.

"Companies are becoming concerned about the export outlook and this is reflected by the fall in optimism about export prospects and the rise in the proportion of companies reporting that prices are a constraint on their ability to win export orders."
The pound has risen in value by around 18 percent against the German mark since last August.
Twenty-three percent of firms reported higher export orders over the past four months and 24 percent reported lower orders, a negative balance of one percent.
Wading into the debate about British monetary policy, the CBI said it saw no immediate need for a rise in official interest rates from the present 6.0 percent.

"This was discussed at some length within the economic affairs committee...and the conclusions were that whilst it was finely balanced, no action was necessary at this time," Buckland told Reuters Financial Television.
Bank of England Governor Eddie George warned the government on Monday night that it would be dangerous to delay a rise in interest rates just because the strong pound was helping to dampen inflation.

Warning that strong growth in money supply and consumer spending could not be sustained for long without jeopardising the government's 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation, George called for a "modest pre-emptive" increase in rates.

His remarks put him at odds with Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke, who said last week that the strength of the pound was one of the key factors that had prompted him to leave interest rates unchanged this month.
A strong pound has the twin effect of making British goods more expensive abroad, while helping to reduce inflation by making it cheaper for British companies to buy imported goods.
With an election due by May 22, Clarke is reluctant to raise interest rates as this would mean dearer mortgages for millions of home-owners.
Money supply figures for December showed M4, widely seen as a pointer to future inflationary pressures, unexpectedly fell 0.2 percent from November on a seasonally adjusted basis.
The annual growth rate slowed to 9.6 percent from 10.8 percent in November, but this was still outside the government's three to nine percent monitoring range.

However, much of the deceleration was due to end-of-year distortions on the "repo" -- sale and repurchase -- market for British government bonds and economists predicted that George would not be deterred from calling for higher interest rates.
